entry.title: Risk of irrelevance?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Risk of irrelevance?Risk of irrelevance?

The scale of the selling and the speed and magnitude of the underperformance in Indian equities are unsustainable

premium

Foreign portfolio investors have withdrawn $65 billion from Indian equities since September 2024, amid sharp market underperformance and declining global investor interest. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Akash Prakash6 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:19 AM ISTI have been investing in Indian equities for over 30 years. Rarely have I seen foreign sentiment this bad. India no longer features in global conversations. What I am saying is not new. Since the Indian market’s peak in September 2024, we have seen $65 billion in net outflows by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Over the last decade, India has received zero net-foreign flows.  The stock of Indian equities owned by foreigners has fallen from $930 billion to about $675 billion, and foreign ownership as a percentage of the market is now at a 15-year low. India is now a consensus underweight for all global investors and our weighting itself has shrunk from 21 per cent in September 2024 to about 10 per cent today (MSCI Emerging Market index).  One company, TSMC, has a benchmark weight 50 per cent higher than that of all of India! The three EM heavyweights — TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix — together account for 30 per cent of the index, but have almost three times India’s weighting.  We have also seen unprecedented underperformance. Since the peak in September 2024, Indian equities are down about 25 per cent in dollar terms, even as the EM indices are up about 50 per cent. We have, therefore, underperformed by 7,500 basis points (75 percentage points) in the last two years alone. I have never in my career seen this quantum of underperformance in this short a period. It has destroyed careers and blown up funds. There are numerous funds that have destroyed 10-year track records in the last 24 months by simply being overweight India.  Normally, I would look at these statistics and numbers as contrarian indicators. This is exactly why I would argue — and still do — that we will soon see a turnaround in India’s relative and absolute performance. The scale of the selling and the speed and magnitude of the underperformance are unsustainable. How can three companies in Asia have three times the index weight of a country with India’s size and potential?  How can these three companies have a combined index weight of 30 per cent, almost identical to the combined weight of India and China, at 30.5 per cent? Something is clearly wrong. It seems ludicrous that three Asian technology companies can have an index weight almost equivalent to 40 per cent of the world’s population. A classic contrarian indicator, if there ever was one.  However, what troubles me is that for the first time I am now being asked about the need for an India-dedicated allocation. Many allocators no longer think India is important enough to warrant dedicated exposure. Why bother with sticking their neck out and betting on India specifically, especially given the extent of underperformance. This conversation has come up now after years. Twenty years ago, every allocator had dedicated money in China and Brazil, and India was a debate. Over time, it became conventional wisdom that to invest in EM, you needed dedicated pools of capital for India, greater China and Brazil. If allocators are now unwilling to make an India-specific bet, it is a big negative and will constrain the quantum of foreign equity as well as the diversity of capital into the country. Non-dedicated exposure by definition is more cyclical.  So why this change in thinking? First of all, it is the decline in India’s EM weighting. At only 10 per cent, we are half what we used to be and three countries — Taiwan, Korea and China — are 70 per cent of the EM index. Do you really need to bother with India? Even getting India wrong will not really move the needle. Over the last 10 years, India has anyway underperformed the EM indices by about 180 basis points annually. Even on a 20-year basis, India has just marginally outperformed. The narrative that you need to be in India because of the quality of companies, sustainability of growth and entrepreneurial energy is getting lost. There is fundamentally less belief that we have decades of strong growth ahead of us.  Second, many investors have come to the conclusion that India may not deliver enough absolute returns. Their calculations are as follows. The Nifty index in rupees has delivered about 10.5 per cent per annum over the last 20 years. Assuming a capital gains tax impact of about 15 per cent (the average of the short-term rate of 20 per cent and the long-term rate of 12.5 per cent), this brings the return down to about 8.9 per cent. Then, assuming a near 4 per cent rupee depreciation (the average over the last 20 years), this brings the return down to about 6 per cent in dollar terms.  Why bother with 6 per cent when the 100-year annualised returns in US equities are about 10 per cent? I would argue that 25-year Nifty returns are near 13.5 per cent not 10 per cent. Nifty returns understate market returns and assuming continued 4 per cent currency depreciation makes no sense given the narrowing inflation differentials. Also, given the valuations, can you assume continued 10 per cent compounding in the United States? However, it does not matter what I think, this is what investors are saying.  All allocators are upset about the capital gains tax. They do not pay these taxes in any other major jurisdiction. It drops projected long-term annualised returns by about 2 per cent and that is a huge difference when comparing countries over long holding periods. There is also the perception that India remains a complex place to do business. Indian service providers do a good job of scaring the risk and compliance teams of global investors. While this may be unfair, the perception sticks.  India is also seen as the biggest global loser from artificial intelligence (AI), as our key advantages of demographics and a skilled white-collar workforce lose relevance in an AI-first world. Innovation and research & development, which are driving value creation globally, are seen as areas of weakness in India. One can refute this argument, but many allocators believe it.  India is also caught in a no-man’s land, not cheap enough for value investors to pile in but not growing fast enough to attract growth investors either.  If India were to lose its attraction as an independent asset class that is a cause of worry. We will attract less structural capital and be of less relevance to global allocators. Not a good place to be for a country fundamentally short of capital. Equity markets are a competitive advantage for India, we weaken this if we lose access to dedicated pools of long-term capital.  I remain convinced that all this data is more a contrarian indicator and not a reason to turn more negative on India. Much of this is cyclical and the tide will turn. However, we must guard against slipping further down the investor consideration set in the meantime.

entry.title: Uneasy lies the governance space
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Uneasy lies the governance spaceUneasy lies the governance space

The ripples the Tata affair will cause are yet to become clear - but promoters will be nervous at such a coup by the professional hire

premium

The governance tensions at Tata Sons have raised questions about promoter control, board independence and the balance of power between shareholders and professional management. | Photo: File

Rama Bijapurkar5 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:05 PM ISTL’affaire Tata Sons has brought into focus the uneasy space between promoters, professional managers, and boards, that India Inc constantly negotiates. While there has not been much public comment from India Inc on the situation (and this columnist rushes in where angels fear to tread), there has been enormous private speculation about how this situation came to pass, and nervous conjecture on what the ripple effects of this will be in shaping the future governance space.   This is neither a spat among shareholder groups for control, nor a summary sacking of a chief executive officer by a promoter. We have seen those movies before. This is almost the first time that a professional manager-CEO, with the board on his side and non-shareholder government institutions weighing in, has sought to marginalise a 66 per cent-owning promoter in decision choices that impact not just the direction of the business (though we are not explicitly hearing from either side about strategic fault lines), but also the promoter’s shareholding.   While CEOs pushing back publicly and openly fighting shareholders is common in bastions of capitalism like the United States, with widely distributed shareholding and boards playing a greater fiduciary role, in India such battles are rare, especially if it is a promoter shareholder. Indian promoters hold the hallowed place of a company’s birth parents with special rights and responsibilities — some enshrined in law, others in culture.   ITC and Larsen & Toubro (L&T) are two unforgettable examples in India of CEO-shareholder battles. In the case of ITC, the battle was against promoter BAT’s  (British American Tobacco’s) move to gain control of the company and stop diversification, while in the case of L&T, it was against a dominant shareholder group, with the CEO fighting to retain management control. In both cases, the government backed the CEO, but by weighing in through its 30 to 40 per cent shareholding via financial institutions it controlled, keeping within the legitimate norm of capitalism: Jiski lathi, uski bhains (whoever has the stick owns the buffalo).   What makes the present Tata Sons case different is that government-controlled entities do not own large chunks of shares, and the duelling ground is not an annual general meeting or extraordinary general meeting. That a CEO with no shareholding backing, along with board members who do not represent chunks of shareholding, can challenge a promoter with a 66 per cent holding and pressure it to dilute its stake, and not have sway over decisions is a first-time challenge to power structures — which have stood the test of time, tradition, convention, and culture, rightly or wrongly. It brings a fresh round of calibration, especially by promoters, of their terms of endearment and engagement with professional CEOs, not to mention boards. More so, if their shareholding is well below 51 per cent.  The relationship between professional managers and promoters in India has always had a degree of tension. The differences that typically end in the CEO quitting could be on several dimensions —differences in direction, risk appetite and prudence, business ambition, remuneration (less so of late as CEO salaries and stock options have zoomed upwards) and often over different perceptions of where the power to make what kind of decisions rests — the birth parent or the foster parent. Human resources consultants frequently counsel boards and CEOs that once the chemistry with the promoter has gone sour, there is no salvaging the relationship.   The separation of management from ownership is not common in India yet, though nascent examples are emerging. Big stock market influencers welcome owner presence in management because they feel a reassuring common focus on increasing shareholder value.  Many employees also prefer a promoter at the helm, seeing this as offering more predictability and benevolence than the CEO or the board of the day. Even in a company like Infosys,  set up by professionals, the “founders” (as they preferred to be called) took turns in running the company in accordance with their pre-agreed plan. The board went along with the frequent changes at the top, presumably because these were the promoters who had built an amazing company and it seemed only fair that they each had their turn.   Given the promoter-friendly, promoter-respectful and promoter-on-top ethos of corporate governance that has existed and continues to exist in India, this departure from the norm against none other than the venerated, iconic Tata promoter group with its track record of trusteeship and larger good over personal gain has rocked the comfort boat all around.  The ripples it will cause are yet to become clear — will promoters be nervous seeing such a coup by the professional hire? How will they respond? Will they pick boards like in the old days, based on loyalty and narrow subject-matter expertise? Especially as the law of the land and the market regulator push more power and accountability in the hands of independent directors? Will boards be now placed under more pressure from external directives on which way to vote, getting trapped between the rock and the hard place of the promoter and the proverbial hand of God? Will CEOs have less freedom to operate and more fetters? And does this add to the bad rap that India has been getting of late as a safe, stable place to invest in for the long term? Probably yes to all.  Since one big pillar of the argument is the national and systemic importance of Tata Sons, its board perhaps needs to be more transparent on the rationale for its many volte-faces.

entry.title: Advance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implications
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Advance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implicationsAdvance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implications

Experts clarify rules on overseas job work under advance authorisation, leasing capital goods under EPCG and timelines for invoicing and export shipments

premium

Exporters must comply with customs and GST rules for overseas job work and shipments (Representative Image)

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:05 AM ISTWe have an export order for an item. We have imported the materials required for manufacturing the item duty free under an advance authorisation. One of our machines to carry out a specialised process has broken down. It will take quite some time to send the machine abroad for repairs and get it back. Our customer cannot wait that long. So, we want to send the imported duty-free material abroad to get the specialised process done and re-import it for further manufacture at our factory. We refer to Paragraph 4.33 of the Handbook of Procedures (HBP), which allows the endorsement of the name of the supporting manufacturer in an advance authorisation. Can we get endorsement of the name of a supporting manufacturer abroad and if so, what are the tax implications?  Para 4.33 of the HBP does not expressly restrict endorsement only to supporting manufacturers or job workers located in India. You can therefore seek endorsement of the overseas job worker’s name and address, explaining that the materials will return to India for further manufacture and subsequent export towards discharge of the export obligation. The proviso to condition (xii) of notification number 21/2023-Customs permits transfer of imported materials for job work subject to the relevant GST (Goods and Services Tax) conditions. Those provisions do not expressly prohibit overseas job work. You should comply with the applicable job-work-challan, recordkeeping, reporting and return-period requirements, and declare the purpose of the temporary export in the shipping bill. On re-import, the processed goods will attract duty under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962, read with any applicable exemption notification. The original duty-free import under the Advance Authorisation does not necessarily exempt this re-import. The invoice of the foreign job-worker will not attract IGST on reverse charge basis because where the specialized process is performed entirely abroad on goods physically made available to the foreign job worker, the place of supply is outside the taxable territory in accordance with Section 13(3)(a) of the IGST Act, 2017.  In the previous Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), capital goods could be imported under Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) even if the same were financed by a leasing company. In the current FTP 2023, there is no such provision. Can we import capital goods on lease basis and clear under EPCG scheme even in current policy 2023?  Para 2.33 of the FTP permits import of capital goods under lease financing without specific DGFT permission. Also, the current definition of ‘importer’ in the Customs Act, 1962 covers the lessee even for import under the EPCG scheme.  Our customer wants us to raise the invoice but delay export shipment by two months. Can we do that?  Yes. Section 31(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017 requires you to raise the invoice before or at the time of removal. However, Rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017 requires you to export the goods removed under Letter of Undertaking or bond within three months from the date of invoice (not removal from the factory). The Commissioner may extend the period.

entry.title: Return of SEZ goods: Welcome relief, unresolved issues
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Return of SEZ goods: Welcome relief, unresolved issuesReturn of SEZ goods: Welcome relief, unresolved issues

The government's new SEZ rules allow customs duty refunds on goods returned after failed deliveries, but a short deadline and unresolved drawback disputes leave gaps for domestic buyers and exporters

premium

Goods returned from Special Economic Zones to the domestic market may qualify for customs duty refunds under the amended rules

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 11:44 PM ISTThe government has amended Rule 49(2) of the Special Economic Zones (SEZ) Rules, 2006, providing for refund of Customs duty when domestic tariff area (DTA) buyers return duty-paid goods to SEZ units following failure to  take delivery. The relief is  welcome but restrictive and leaves unresolved disputes over drawback claims relating to earlier returns.  The notification dated October 15, 2026, covers cases where a DTA buyer fails to take delivery because of changes in fashion, market conditions or default in conditions of the sale agreement. The goods must return within thirty days of clearance. The DTA buyer who paid or bore the duty can claim refund under Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962. The goods must be identified to the satisfaction of the specified officer and evidence furnished that the DTA buyer has not availed any benefits, including input tax credit (ITC). The SEZ unit must furnish that evidence and maintain a separate auditable inventory of returned goods. The amendment permits SEZ units to resell returned goods in their original condition to the same or another DTA buyer, on payment of applicable duties as a fresh sale. The repair facility is retained.  Previously, Rule 49(2) allowed return of goods supplied by SEZ units only for repairs. It contained no express provision for refund on failed deliveries. The new provision addresses a practical difficulty faced by domestic buyers and SEZ suppliers. However, thirty days from clearance is a short period for resolving a failed delivery and arranging return. There is no express provision for extending the deadline. More importantly, the wording covers a buyer who fails to take delivery, leaving doubt about goods rejected after delivery. The explanation below S.No.15 of Annexure-I to notification 52/2003-Cus dated March 31, 2003, relating to export-oriented units (EOUs) clarifies that failure of the foreign buyer to take delivery includes rejection of goods by that buyer. A similar explanation should be inserted now to cover rejection by DTA buyers. The requirement that no benefits should have been availed also leaves unclear whether ITC initially taken but subsequently reversed will suffice. This too needs clarification.  The amendment operates prospectively. Earlier, DTA buyers filed drawback bills of export under Section 74 of the Customs Act when returning identifiable, duty-paid goods to SEZ units. Customs disputed some claims because the definition of export under the Customs Act and the 1995 Re-export Drawback Rules did not include DTA supplies to SEZs. CBIC Instruction No.06/2026-Customs, dated April 27, 2026, recognised SEZ clearances into DTA as imports for Section 74 drawback purposes. However, it did not expressly address whether sending goods from DTA to SEZ qualifies as export for that section. This issue affects both returns of goods procured from SEZs and supplies of goods originally imported from abroad. The controversy persists despite Section 2(m)(ii) of the SEZ Act, 2005, recognising DTA supplies to SEZ units for authorised operations as exports, and Section 51 giving that Act overriding effect where other laws are inconsistent.  The government should allow more time for returns, empower authorities to extend the deadline, and provide refund of duty for goods returned for any reason, with safeguards. It should clarify that Section 74 drawback is available on duty-paid imported goods sent to SEZs. Prospective relief should be accompanied by resolution of past disputes on the same issue.

entry.title: Market reforms: The unfinished agenda
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Market reforms: The unfinished agendaMarket reforms: The unfinished agenda

Consistent publication of dispute rulings, standardised document requirements for claims and a name-based search facility could help families trace unclaimed mutual fund investments

premium

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 11:05 PM ISTRatan, a friend, was buying his dream home. The seller had brought the registration forward by a day, and his mutual fund redemption money was now due on that very day. He needed it in the morning to get a pay order for the afternoon appointment. His question was simple. At what time would the money reach his bank account? By 8 am, it had. What struck me was that his worry had been about the hour. He had taken the date for granted.  Anyone who invested in shares a few decades ago will understand why Ratan’s confidence struck me. Payments could be delayed, and physical share transfers could get stuck for months over signature mismatches. Today, trades settle the next working day and shares arrive directly in your demat account. With the UPI block facility, your money can stay in your bank account earning interest until needed for a purchase. Scams and payment crises prompted many of these changes, often after investors had paid dearly. Each reform meant changing practices that somebody benefited from.  The confidence these reforms have helped build is particularly visible in mutual funds. Entry loads, deducted from your money before it was even invested, were abolished in 2009. Direct plans followed in 2013, allowing investors to avoid distributor commissions. Clearer scheme categories made funds easier to understand and compare, while the riskometer showed how risky each scheme is. Investors now put over ₹32,000 crore every month through systematic investment plans (SIPs), with investments held through SIPs worth nearly ₹18 lakh crore. This confidence was built while openly acknowledging the risks. Advertisements repeatedly reminded investors that mutual fund investments are subject to market risk and returns are not guaranteed.  The improvements extend to families claiming investments after a death. Your family can now report the death to a single intermediary, and the other intermediaries must contact the nominee with the procedure and documents required. We saw this work smoothly when a deceased client’s family received his mutual funds and shares within 10 days of submitting documents.   But families can still face unreasonable demands where there is no nominee or surviving joint holder. While claiming my late father’s unclaimed shares, I was asked for my mother’s death certificate from 1963. Families need predictable document requirements in every case.  An arbitrator on the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (Sebi’s) Online Dispute Resolution (SMART ODR) platform ruled in my favour on that demand. But why should the next investor have to fight the same battle? Publishing decisions with personal details removed would help investors understand their rights and discourage intermediaries from repeating unreasonable demands. Sebi already requires this publication, but it is not done consistently. And if analysis shows the same complaint recurring, the cause should be fixed rather than each case fought one by one.   Then there is money that families have lost track of. Unclaimed mutual fund dividends and redemption proceeds were ₹3,811 crore as on March 31, 2026. MITRA (Mutual Fund Investment Tracing and Retrieval Assistant) helps trace inactive folios, but only if you have the investment details. How can the children provide those details when they do not even know whether the parent invested in mutual funds? The Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) allows a search for unclaimed shares by name. A similar search across mutual funds would let children start with a parent’s name and discover whether anything is lying unclaimed. The usual worry is fraud. But entitlement is checked before payment, so fraud by a few should not stop families from claiming what is rightfully theirs.   Truth be told, the confidence Ratan has was built one reform at a time. The remaining gaps can be closed the same way, and none needs new technology or a new law. Sebi can ensure that ODR decisions are published, as its own rules already require. It can lay down one complete list of documents for claims, beyond which nothing may be asked. And it can allow a name search for unclaimed mutual fund money, as IEPF already does for shares. Ratan worried only about the hour. Every investor deserves the same confidence.

entry.title: The neglected species of pulses
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The neglected species of pulsesThe neglected species of pulses

Reviving neglected pulses could boost nutrition, reduce imports and improve farmers' incomes

premium

Underutilised pulses could strengthen India’s nutritional security while supporting farmers and reducing import dependence

Surinder Sud5 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:46 PM ISTIn a country where pulses (dal) are the major source of protein for most people, malnutrition is rampant, and import dependence for meeting pulses requirements is substantial, the suboptimal utilisation of the existing diversity of indigenous legumes is hard to justify. Only eight of the available 14 species of pulses are grown and consumed on a regular basis. The others (leguminous crops) have either been abandoned or are cultivated and consumed in specific areas on a small scale. Many of these underexploited species have impressive nutritional profiles. Their mainstreaming can be a boon to consumers, as also to small and marginal farmers, who have traditionally been growing these hardy and drought-resistant crops in arid, semi-arid, and degraded lands, but have stopped doing so because of waning market demand.  These underutilised species include Moth bean (Moth dal), Lathyrus (Khesari dal), Horse gram (Kulthi), Faba bean (Bakla or Kala matar), Rice bean (Sutri or Lal bean), and Adzuki bean (Lal mung or Lal chowri). Their farming is confined to limited areas, chiefly for local consumption. Going by their merits, in terms of versatility, ease of cultivation, and health benefits, these deserve better usage.  Unfortunately, these species of pulses have been neglected even by agricultural scientists and are, therefore, often dubbed as “orphan crops”. Not enough research & development has been done to improve their productivity, grain quality, processability, and marketability by developing superior high-yielding crop strains. Such apathy towards these valuable legumes is unwarranted, given the dire need to augment the availability of protein-dense foods to strengthen nutritional security.  The country’s pulses sector is dominated by just five legumes, which together account for 90 per cent of production and consumption. These are pigeon pea (tur or arhar), chickpea (chana or gram), green gram (mung), black gram (urad), and lentil (masoor). The bulk of the remaining 10 per cent consumption is shared by three pulses – red kidney beans (Rajma), black eyed peas (Lobiya), and field peas (Matar).  There are, indeed, several good reasons for harnessing the untapped potential of the little-used pulses. For one, these can boost the domestic supply of legumes to reduce pulses imports, which amounted to 7 million tonnes in 2024-25 and 6 million tonnes in 2025-26. Besides, these pulses can grow on poor-quality lands not ideally suited for cultivating main cereals and commercial crops. In fact, being leguminous crops, these can improve the fertility of such lands by fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. These crops can, therefore, serve virtually as an effective means of regenerating degraded lands, which abound in India, spanning over 98 million hectares. Moreover, these crops, requiring little investment in cash inputs, can be a vital livelihood support for resource-starved farmers owning such lands. And most importantly, they are regarded by farm scientists as a repository of genes that might prove useful in imparting climate change-resilience, immunity against diseases and pests, and other desirable traits, in future crop species.  Interestingly, most of these underexploited crops possess significant amounts of dietary fibre and bioactive compounds, which can mitigate the challenges posed by the rising incidence of lifestyle and flawed nutrition-induced ailments, such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, cardiovascular diseases, and even cancer.  The reasons for these species of pulses falling out of favour, though formidable, are not difficult to overcome. Many of their drawbacks can be remedied through simple treatment and managerial intervention, such as soaking in water or processing them into value-added products to prepare nutritious snacks. In the case of Moth bean, for instance, the main problem is the long time it takes to cook. This can easily be cut down to half by soaking the grains in water overnight. Preparing in a pressure cooker can reduce it further.  The Khesari dal, which has a very high protein content of 26-28 per cent, was temporarily banned because of the rise in the incidence of neurological disorder called lathyrism (paralysis of lower limbs) among its regular consumers in regions like Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh. Scientific studies later revealed that this condition was caused due to the presence of a neurotoxin, called beta-ODAP, in Khesari dal, and affected primarily those who ate this cheapest available legume almost as a staple. Studies also showed that the problem could be largely solved by soaking it in salt water, and discarding the water. This lowers the toxin level down to almost safe limits, especially if consumed in moderation.  Sprouting is another simple and effective way of improving the digestibility of these less used pulses, and also their acceptability among people. It activates their internal enzymes, which transform these grains into nutritional powerhouses.  There is, thus, a strong case for making better use of the underexploited legumes to enhance the overall availability of pulses. The Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, set up last year to make the country self-sufficient in pulses by 2030-31, would hopefully do the needful in this direction.

entry.title: Can your refrigerator be hacked?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Can your refrigerator be hacked?Can your refrigerator be hacked?

Consumers and corporations will have to be as careful about protecting appliances as they are with office equipment, like computers and servers

premium

Any connected device deserves enterprise-level cybersecurity protocols | Representative Picture

Pranjal Sharma4 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTBeing smart can be a weakness, especially for everyday appliances that are part of daily lives. As machines, appliances and devices get more connected, they provide increasing ease of use.   Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens, microwaves, dishwashers, washing machines, and air conditioners are no longer just standalone household devices. They are increasingly connected to the internet, mobile apps, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems to improve convenience, energy efficiency, safety, and food management.  A smart refrigerator can monitor internal temperatures, alert users if the door is left open, track inventory through cameras or barcode scanning, and suggest recipes based on available ingredients. Some advanced models from companies such as Samsung and LG can synchronise with grocery shopping apps, create shopping lists, and even automatically reorder frequently used products.  However, this connectivity can be weaponised to convert the appliances into devices of destruction. Appliances placed in homes, restaurants, offices, industrial sites and government buildings are no longer harmless tools of convenience. Connected household appliances such as smart refrigerators, microwaves, ovens, televisions, cameras, and thermostats have become increasingly attractive targets for cybercriminals, because they often have internet connectivity, but weaker security controls than traditional computers. Security experts have repeatedly demonstrated that these devices can be compromised and used as entry points into broader home or enterprise networks.  An early case occurred in 2014, when researchers discovered a botnet composed of internet-connected devices, including smart refrigerators and televisions, that had been hijacked to send hundreds of thousands of spam emails. The recent hacking of fridges of supermarket chains in France has revived fears of hacked appliances.   French supermarket chains, including Intermarché, E.Leclerc, and Système U lost millions worth of frozen food, after attackers gained access to refrigeration management systems and remotely altered temperature settings.   The attackers targeted refrigeration control technology, changing settings so that refrigeration units continuously defrosted and temperatures reportedly rose as high as 50°C, effectively turning cooling systems into heaters.  Many more unnoticed hacks are occurring across millions of connected devices. Industry data indicates that the threat environment is worsening. Research from Bitdefender and NETGEAR found that the average connected household experienced approximately 29 cyberattacks per day in 2025, with attacks increasingly targeting consumer electronics such as smart TVs, streaming devices, cameras, and other connected appliances. The study observed billions of attack attempts across millions of households, highlighting how smart home devices have become routine targets for automated cybercriminal activity. Smart appliances can enable indirect surveillance. A connected refrigerator, thermostat, smart lighting system, or washing machine may reveal occupancy patterns, sleep schedules, vacation periods, or daily routines through usage logs. Even without accessing cameras or microphones, an attacker who obtains this data may be able to determine when people are home, asleep, or away.  Connected appliances placed in commercial locations and government offices can be used for spying and gathering data. Connected building controls, refrigeration systems, industrial sensors, and surveillance devices can provide information about operating schedules, facility utilisation, inventory levels, and employee activity. Smart speakers represent another potential hacking concern. While devices such as Amazon Echo, Google Nest, and Apple HomePod are designed to activate only after hearing a wake word, security researchers have demonstrated techniques that can manipulate voice assistants or exploit software vulnerabilities to gather information or trigger actions. More commonly, privacy concerns arise from the amount of voice and behavioral data stored in cloud systems, rather than from direct hacking.  Consumers and corporations will have to be as careful about protecting appliances as they are with office equipment, like computers and servers. If a smart appliance is connected to the same router as the enterprise, it offers a vulnerable entry point for hacking the entire system. Hacking a fridge in an inhouse café of a large corporation can be as risky as hacking a laptop or a mobile device. Any connected device, from a wrist watch to a washing machine, deserves enterprise level cyber security protocols.    Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Ten rules for external sector stress
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Ten rules for external sector stressTen rules for external sector stress

There is wisdom from history in managing the rupee

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ajay ShahK P KrishnanG Padmanabhan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTThere is considerable stress in the Indian external sector. Policymakers see information that we, as external persons, do not. From the outside, it is not useful to comment on the minutiae of tactical policy moves. Drawing on the experiences of crises in the Indian external sector over the past 25 years, we offer 10 principles that are universally useful in understanding the present situation and responding to it.  1. Supply stability, not shocks. Policymakers must be a supplier of stability, not the originator — whether intended or otherwise — of shocks. We should plan every action of policymakers to be calm, reassuring, and predictable. The dharma of modern central banking is “say what you will do and then do what you just said”. Surprises should emanate from the external world — such as the October 14 Houthi attack upon Saudi Aramco in Dhahran — not from the authorities.  2. Leave price discovery to private persons. Speculating about financial prices is the work of private persons, not the Indian state. There will always be legitimate disagreement about what values of the rupee will be, and state agencies should not be put in a position of having to take a stand on this. Getting into dogfights with speculators is problematic. Speculators are a formidable force. Tangling with them is daunting. In addition, policymakers lose strategic sense when they are enveloped in a fog of war. They should be above the fray of the practical details of what is happening in the market: The buying, the selling, and the price.  3. Respect the scale of cross-border flows. The Indian economy is very big, and the money moving across the border is now vast. In 2025-26, gross flows on the current account were $2.18 trillion, while gross private flows on the capital and financial account were $3.21 trillion. Thus, over $5.39 trillion comes in and goes out of India every year. Every dollar out of this is in the command of self-interested and intelligent people who are watching the landscape and trying to earn a profit from currency speculation when opportunities present themselves. When currency speculation through financial instruments becomes difficult, this activity goes into the behaviour of foreign direct investment (FDI), imports, exports, and remittances. The adjustment that is prevented on the exchange rate is concentrated in domestic asset prices.  4. Financial development has hysteresis. It cannot be turned off and on like a tap. A good financial system is ultimately about the emergence of capable teams in Indian and foreign financial firms. Those draw upon decades of investment and sustained knowledge building. When a market’s or a product’s life ends, we lose decades of culture. The threat of future bans lurks in the mind of decision-makers in private financial firms. They respond by investing less in organisational capabilities. This results in a less knowledgeable and less capable financial sector. This is harmful for India. It creates conditions of excess volatility in illiquid financial markets.  5. Get on to the virtuous cycle. Good countries get on to the virtuous cycle of high financial development, high market liquidity, and reduced volatility. However, there can also be the opposite feedback loop: Government management of a price leads to damaged financial development, market illiquidity, greater volatility, and then pressure upon the government to intervene in prices.  6. Treat cross-border friction in a unified way. Indian economic growth is made in the most productive firms, and the most productive firms are the internationalised ones. A firm does not experience each regulatory obstacle in isolation; rules across trade, capital, data, and payments interact as one connected system that shapes how investors judge Indian governance. When greater cross-border friction comes about — against the movement of money across the border, against currency trading, against currency-risk management, against internationalised business activities — these are harmful for Indian economic growth. When we make capital flows and risk management more difficult, this harms stock prices and the exchange rate, as the foreigner demands a higher risk premium.  7. Avoid currency dominance. Every currency defence turns into an interest-rate defence. This induces a loss of autonomy in monetary policy. For decades, Indian economic policy worked to protect monetary policy from “fiscal dominance”, where the short-term interest rate was controlled by the fiscal deficit. We should not now relapse into “currency dominance”. The short-term interest rate should be shaped by inflation forecasts alone, and not get distorted by currency considerations. The 91-day bill went up by about 50 basis points in a month; we should ask whether this conduct was optimal from the viewpoint of the 4 per cent inflation target.  8. Intellectual power beats coercive power. Policymakers are judged every day by the market for the internal consistency and feasibility of their efforts, and for their intellectual capabilities. Policymaking viewed as a power game works poorly as, ultimately, the global financial system is more powerful than the Indian policymaker. The soft power of respect in the eyes of the people who shape business and finance strategy worldwide matters more.  9. Renew vows to the reform strategy. There is only one configuration that is consistent with Indian success: Inflation targeting, a floating exchange rate, and an open capital account. Policymakers need to renew their vows to this strategic picture of Indian economic reforms every few weeks. Reversals of reforms are generally avoidable, they should be accompanied by an apology, and they should concern minor things.  10. Emulate the good countries. There are countries that are basket cases, like Russia or Turkey. India should aim to be like the good ones, like South Korea, Taiwan or Israel, which maintain low cross-border friction across trade, capital, technology, data, and finance. We need to self-consciously up our game and match their policy frameworks, their everyday stream of policy decisions and communication, and their body language.
The writers are, respectively, a researcher at XKDR Forum; an honorary senior fellow at the Isaac Centre for Public Policy, and a former civil servant; and former executive director, Reserve Bank of India     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: From PCA to Prem Watsa: IDBI Bank's long road to privatisation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / From PCA to Prem Watsa: IDBI Bank's long road to privatisationFrom PCA to Prem Watsa: IDBI Bank's long road to privatisation

Banks in a growing economy need patient, long-term foreign capital with good governance to meet credit demand

premium

For IDBI Bank, the February 2021 Budget announced the government's plan for strategic disinvestment; an in-principle Cabinet approval followed in May 2021 (Photo: Bloomberg)

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 9:53 PM ISTWhat do IDBI Bank Ltd and Air India have in common? For both, privatisation turned into a five-year plan. Of course, the erstwhile Planning Commission is not involved in their cases!  Following Cabinet approval in June 2017, the government invited expressions of interest (EoIs) for Air India in March 2018, offering a 76 per cent stake, but it drew no bids. A revised plan offering 100 per cent was launched in January 2020; the Tata Group won the bid in October 2021 and took over the airline in January 2022.  For IDBI Bank, the February 2021 Budget announced the government's plan for strategic disinvestment; an in-principle Cabinet approval followed in May 2021. EoIs were invited in October 2022.  In March 2023, the then Department of Investment and Public Asset Management Secretary Tuhin Kanta Pandey (now chairman of the capital market regulator) tweeted: "Reports appearing in a section of the media indicating the possibility of deferment of IDBI Bank disinvestment are misleading… The transaction continues to be on track as per the defined process in the post-EoI stage following receipts of multiple EoIs."  In March 2026, the government called off the first round after financial bids from Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd and Emirates NBD fell short of the reserve price. Revised bids came in by July 2026.  On October 14, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved Canada's Fairfax as the strategic buyer. Fairfax will buy the 60.72 per cent stake (30.48 per cent from the government and 30.24 per cent from Life Insurance Corporation of India, or LIC) for ₹52,878 crore. This will be the largest foreign direct investment in the history of India's financial sector. The deal is expected to close by March 2027, once all approvals are in place.  Fairfax plans to bring IDBI Bank, Go Digit Insurance, and IIFL Capital Services Ltd under one umbrella, creating a large integrated financial group on Indian turf. Fairfax is the controlling promoter of Go Digit General Insurance Ltd. Its stake in IIFL Capital is 30.2 per cent, and it is in the process of raising it to 51 per cent.  It also holds 40 per cent in CSB Bank Ltd. We don't know where CSB Bank fits into Fairfax's scheme of things. It may merge it with IDBI Bank or sell its stake to another investor. It has a two-year window to resolve the overlap.  Indeed, the IDBI Bank privatisation took a long time, but it is yet another signal of how the approach of the government and the banking regulator to the financial sector is changing.  Once upon a time, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was looking for a suitor for United Western Bank Ltd. Standard Chartered Bank was among 17 contenders, but an acquisition by a foreign bank was a big no-no in the RBI's playbook in those days. In 2006, the Satara-based old private bank was merged with IDBI Bank.  Before that, HSBC had acquired a 20 per cent stake in UTI Bank Ltd (now Axis Bank Ltd) in December 2003. Under the RBI's ownership norms, it had to pare its stake to below 5 per cent in 2006, and it eventually exited in 2012, nearly a decade after the acquisition.  Things started changing in the middle of the last decade. In December 2016, the RBI allowed Fairfax to take a majority stake in Catholic Syrian Bank Ltd, the first time a foreign investor had been permitted to control an Indian bank. Fairfax recapitalised it, renamed it CSB Bank, and listed it on the bourses in 2019.  Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) holds 24.99 per cent in Yes Bank Ltd. Dubai-based Emirates NBD completed the acquisition of a 60 per cent controlling stake in RBL Bank Ltd in June 2026.  Among other large single investors, Warburg Pincus has close to 10 per cent of IDFC First Bank Ltd, and Blackstone will have 9.99 per cent of Federal Bank Ltd once its warrants are converted.  The RBI has progressively raised the voting-rights ceiling for a single shareholder in a private bank from 10 per cent to 26 per cent, and case-by-case exemptions on ownership are made, depending on the circumstances. CSB Bank was the first experiment with such an exemption, and a successful one.  The reasons behind the exemptions differ: Stress at a bank, a strategic goal of building a larger entity, or the government wanting to encash value. In the case of IDBI Bank, the government will get about ₹26,543 crore for its 30.48 per cent. It can make more later, as it will still hold 15 per cent in the bank.  Banks in a growing economy need patient, long-term foreign capital with good governance to meet credit demand. The direction is right.  Overall foreign direct investment (FDI) in private banks is permitted up to 74 per cent – 49 per cent through the automatic route, and investment between 49 and 74 per cent needing government approval. For public sector banks, the FDI ceiling is 20 per cent and government ownership cannot fall below 51 per cent.  It has been a different Diwali for both IDBI Bank and its MD and CEO Rakesh Sharma. He took charge in October 2018, a few weeks before that year's Diwali; eight years on, the strategic sale has come just ahead of another Diwali. Sharma, whose current tenure runs till March 2028, will remain at the helm.  It has not been an easy task.  The RBI placed IDBI Bank under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework in May 2017 because of its high net non-performing assets (NPAs) and negative return on assets. PCA restricted the bank's lending, branch expansion, and hiring.  Nearly one-third of the bank's loan portfolio had turned bad. By September 2018, its gross NPAs were 31.78 per cent, the highest bad-loan ratio ever recorded by an Indian commercial bank. In that quarter, net NPAs were 17.3 per cent, a tad lower than 18.76 per cent in June.  IDBI Bank also holds the record for losses – for 13 successive quarters, between December 2016 and December 2019. During this period, it accumulated net losses of about ₹41,800 crore, driven by massive provisioning for its ballooning NPAs.  Following capital infusions from the government and ₹21,624 crore from LIC, which took a 51 per cent controlling stake in January 2019, the RBI reclassified it as a private sector bank. The bank broke its losing streak in the March 2020 quarter with a net profit of ₹135 crore, and a year later, in March 2021, the PCA restrictions were lifted. After a gap of eight years, it paid a dividend (10 per cent) for FY2023.  Since returning to profit in March 2020, IDBI Bank has not looked back. In the September 2026 quarter, its gross NPAs were 2.12 per cent and net NPAs 0.17 per cent. It made a net profit of ₹2,205 crore in the quarter and ₹4,320 crore in the first half of the current fiscal. Its net interest margin was 4.11 per cent in September, 0.50 percentage point higher than in June.  One contributing factor has been cutting down high-cost bulk deposits.   Meanwhile, the once-corporate lender is now a retail bank, with retail loans accounting for nearly 70 per cent of its ₹2.72 trillion loan book. Finally, its capital adequacy ratio is 27.1 per cent, which means it can grow substantially without raising fresh capital. What else does a bank need?   ____________________________________________________________________________________________________  The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. His latest book: Roller Coaster: An Affair with Banking. To read his previous columns, log on to www.bankerstrust.in. X: @TamalBandyo      Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
